summary: Pilate sends Jesus to Herod Antipas, who hopes to see a miracle; Jesus answers him nothing, and Herod mocks Him and sends Him back.
key_insight: Jesus spoke to Annas, to Caiaphas and to Pilate. To Herod, who had long wanted to see Him and questioned Him with many words, He said nothing at all.
story: When Pilate heard Galilee mentioned, he asked if the Man were a Galilean. As soon as he learned that Jesus belonged to Herod’s jurisdiction, he sent Him to Herod, who was also in Jerusalem at that time.
Herod was exceedingly glad to see Jesus. He had wanted to see Him for a long time, because he had heard many things about Him, and he hoped to see some miracle done by Him.
So Herod questioned Him with many words, but He answered him nothing. All the while the chief priests and scribes stood there and vehemently accused Him.
Then Herod and his soldiers treated Jesus with contempt and mocked Him. They dressed Him in a gorgeous robe and sent Him back to Pilate.
That very day Pilate and Herod became friends with each other. Before that they had been at enmity.

scene.label: Herod’s jurisdiction
scene.text: Galilee belonged to Herod Antipas, not to Pilate, who governed Judea. Pilate could have judged a case that arose in Jerusalem himself. Sending the prisoner to the ruler of his home region was a courtesy, and perhaps a way to pass along a difficult case.

scene.label: In Jerusalem for the feast
scene.text: Antipas ruled for Rome but presented himself as a Jew, and he came up for Passover. Since Pilate probably used Herod the Great’s palace, Antipas probably stayed in the older Hasmonean palace near the temple.

scene.label: A gorgeous robe
scene.text: Luke’s word means bright or shining, the same word used of an angel’s “bright clothing” (Acts 10:30). Herod dressed Jesus as a mock king or royal candidate and sent Him back as a joke.

scene.label: Enemies made friends
scene.text: Luke does not say why the two rulers had been enemies. Pilate’s killing of Galileans (Luke 13:1) may have offended Herod. Philo also tells of Herod’s sons joining a protest to Emperor Tiberius against Pilate; Antipas was probably among them.

witnesses.luke: Only Luke records Jesus before Herod, whose curiosity he has followed since Herod asked, “who is this of whom I hear such things?” (9:9). Luke may have had sources close to Herod’s court, such as Joanna, wife of Herod’s steward (8:3), and Manaen, “brought up with Herod the tetrarch” (Acts 13:1). In Acts the church prays about this day: Herod and Pontius Pilate were gathered together against God’s holy Servant Jesus (Acts 4:27).

seeing.reveals: Jesus will not perform on demand. The One who healed crowds and answered honest questions gives nothing but silence to a ruler who wanted a show and had silenced John the Baptist.
seeing.living: Jesus can be approached for mercy, for truth and for help, but not as entertainment. Herod wanted a miracle and had no interest in repenting. Come to Jesus to be changed, not to be impressed.
seeing.ponder: Do you come to Jesus wanting Him to do something for you, or wanting Him?

preaching.big_idea: Herod wanted a miracle, not a Master, and Jesus gave him silence.
outline: A ruler passing the problem along (6–7)
preaching.watch_for: Herod “sought to see Him” in Luke 9:9, and here he finally does. Acts 4:25–28 reads this day through Psalm 2: the rulers took counsel together against the LORD’s Anointed, yet they did only what God had determined beforehand.
